claims.text: The additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy contains dual nanoprecipitates.
The dual nanoprecipitates are induced by additive manufacturing.
At high temperatures, the dual nanoprecipitates drive elemental segregation.
Nanoprecipitate-driven segregation promotes the formation of protective oxide layers.
The protective oxide layers enhance oxidation resistance relative to cast or wrought samples.
Dual nanoprecipitates can preferentially sequester oxide-forming elements such as Al, Cr, or Ti.
During high-temperature exposure, nanoprecipitates redistribute oxide-forming elements toward grain boundaries and surfaces.
Redistribution of oxide-forming elements toward grain boundaries and surfaces facilitates adherent, protective oxide scales.
APT will reveal a measurable elemental concentration gradient at nanoprecipitate–matrix interfaces.
The interfacial elemental gradient will correlate with reduced oxidation degradation.
The AM alloy will exhibit lower oxidation degradation than conventionally processed versions of the same alloy.
Cast and wrought versions of the alloy lack the additive-manufacturing-induced nanostructure used as the hypothesized mediator.
The redistribution effect will be most pronounced when the nanoscale precipitate structure is well developed.
Other alloy compositions or AM conditions that produce different nanostructures may not show the same redistribution behavior.
Instrumentation limits and processing variability make the magnitude of redistribution and its effect on oxidation kinetics uncertain.
APT can provide three-dimensional elemental maps suitable for comparing segregation at nanoprecipitate–matrix interfaces.
